story:
The apartment complex had said noon, and the odometer said they'd make it with eleven minutes to spare, which Andrew's father treated as a personal triumph and Andrew treated as evidence that the universe was committed to seeing this through. He sat in the back seat with a box of records on his lap because the trunk was full, and every mile marker outside Canton felt like a notch being cut into something. His little sister Priya, thirteen and garrulous in the way of someone who has decided the trip will be unbearable unless she narrates it, had been talking since the county line.

"You could write actual letters," she said now. "People used to do that."

"Nobody did that. You're thinking of movies."

"I'm thinking of Grandma." She kicked the back of his seat, lightly, twice. "You could also just accept that you'll never talk to Danny again and it'll be fine."

"That's a cheery theory."

"It's not a theory. It's a prediction." She paused, then leaned into the gap between the front seats. "Hey, Mom, at orientation they told us about this study. In student housing. 1950. Festinger, Schachter, and Back. They found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends."

Andrew's mother said something agreeable from the front. Andrew looked out the window.

"How do you even remember that," he said.

"Because I thought it was sad. Danny's not going to be near your stairway. He's going to be near some kid named Kyle." She said the name Kyle with the flat cruelty only a thirteen-year-old could manage. "You'll be near some kid named Kyle."

He didn't answer, but the fact stayed with him the way a stone stays in a shoe. He turned it over for forty miles. It seemed to suggest that what he had with Danny, with Marcus, with the whole ragged crowd of them, was not chosen so much as arranged, that the friendship was an accident of geography, two lockers side by side, a cul-de-sac that funneled them together every afternoon until the closeness was indistinguishable from love. He had always believed, privately and without examining it, that he had picked those people, that some quality in him had recognized some quality in them. If the study was right, the picking had been done by a stairwell. He tried to decide whether that made the friendships smaller or the world larger, and couldn't, and the not-knowing sat in his chest alongside the leaving.

His phone buzzed against the box. Danny: are you there yet. Then, before Andrew could type: remember when marcus fell in the creek trying to save that shoe. Andrew laughed out loud, alone in the back seat, and typed back a whole paragraph about the shoe, the look on Marcus's face, the June light on the water. Then he deleted the paragraph, because it felt like a eulogy, and sent instead: we should visit the creek before it gets cold. I'll come back.

Danny's reply came as the exit sign appeared: deal. and you'll meet my new friend kyle probably. he's actually ok. Andrew stared at that. Kyle, apparently, was a person, a person who lived near Danny's stairway now, or near his locker, or whatever the geometry of their junior year was going to be, and Danny was already softening toward him, already being shaped by proximity the way water is shaped by a channel. And wasn't Andrew going to do the same thing? Wasn't there some kid in his own building already, unmet, near his own shared stairway, waiting to be grafted on? He had spent the whole drive thinking of himself as someone being subtracted, and it had not occurred to him until now that he was also being added to something.

"It's not either/or," Priya said, when he said some of this out loud, awkward and halting, because saying it at all cost him something. "The study doesn't say you only like who's nearby. It says you're more likely to become friends with them. Likely. It's not fate, it's odds." She said this with the terrible offhandedness of someone quoting something she'd absorbed without effort, and then ruined it by adding, "Also I already told you this, you weren't listening."

But he had been listening, or at least the fact had been listening for him, and the two ideas began to fit together in a way he could almost hold. The old friendships had been given their chance by a street and a stairwell, yes, by nothing he'd chosen; and still, given that chance, he and Danny had built something on it, had made a thousand decisions small as breath to keep showing up. Proximity was the confounder he'd been blaming, or maybe it was just the door, and doors didn't tell you what to do inside the room. He couldn't prove which it was. He might lose Danny anyway. He might find that some kinds of distance really do thin a thing out, and he would have to stand in his new stairwell, a stranger, and find out what he was without the old arrangement holding him up. He could admit all of that and still send the text he was composing, so he did: saturday after next. i'll take the bus. ask your mom if i can sleep on the couch.

His father pulled into the complex lot at 11:52, and they all sat for a moment while the engine ticked, looking at the pale buildings, the long shared stairways, the doors packed close as teeth. Priya was already unbuckling. Andrew picked up the box of records and got out into the heat, and from the second-floor walkway a boy about his age was carrying a mattress with his father, sweat-dark shirt, and as they passed each other the boy said, "Stairwell C is faster, the elevator's broken." Andrew shifted the box against his hip and said, "Thanks," and then, after a few steps, called back up the stairs, "Hey, what's your name?"

Aiden knelt in the bed at the far end of the garden and pulled a weed that came up with more soil than root, which meant he'd snapped it and would meet it again next week. The Saturday morning had the smell of cut basil and wet cardboard mulch, and someone's radio near the shed was playing a station that seemed to consist entirely of weather reports and gentle disappointment. He was trying to finish weeding before eleven, because at eleven the garden's little folding table was supposed to hold a petition, and the petition was his.

"Is this the thing about Fairmont Road?" asked Rosa, who had the plot beside his and grew more tomatoes than any one household could reasonably want. She was carrying a watering can in each hand like a scale weighing some invisible argument.

"It's the thing about the road eating the garden," Aiden said. The plan the council would vote on next month would widen Fairmont by two lanes and take the garden's southern strip, where the fig tree stood and where the compost sat in various stages of decay, plus the fence and about a third of the plots, his own among them. He smoothed the petition on the table and weighted its corners with four of Rosa's tomato seconds, since no one had thought to bring rocks.

"People want the road wider," Rosa said, not unkindly. "My brother sits in that traffic every day. He says it adds forty minutes to his life, taken out of him one evening at a time."

"I know." Aiden had spent two evenings reading everything the transportation office had posted online, most of it dense enough to be a form of punishment, until he'd found a study from another city where they'd widened a highway and the congestion came back within a few years. He'd read the sentence four times. Faster trips attracted more driving until the new space filled. They had a name for it, and once he had the name he kept finding it everywhere, in articles, in a footnote, in a comment by a planner who sounded tired in a textual way.

By eleven, seven people had signed, and two of those were gardeners who had already signed at the Wednesday meeting, which Rosa counted as fraud until Aiden pointed out it was mostly enthusiasm. Then a man in a polo shirt arrived, council badge clipped crookedly, and stood in the path with his hands in his pockets in the manner of someone who intended to be reasonable at you.

"Councilman Bere," he said. "Just listening today. Nice place." He looked at the fig tree the way one looks at a beloved dog that has chewed something expensive.

Aiden wiped his hands on his jeans and introduced himself, and the conversation went where he'd expected. Congestion, commute times, the will of the voters, growth. "The road is a funnel," Bere said, gesturing with an open palm down the invisible length of Fairmont. "You can't pour more through a narrow funnel. Any polity that grows has to grow its arteries."

The phrase made Aiden oddly bolder, the way a badly chosen metaphor will. "But adding lanes to a congested highway often doesn't reduce traffic for long," he said. "Faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills. It's called induced demand." He heard his own voice land the last two words more loudly than he'd planned, and a pigeon left the fig tree in what felt like editorial comment.

Bere smiled the smile of a man who had been to many meetings. "That's one theory among several, son."

"It's what happened in the study I read," Aiden said, and then, because he wanted to be honest even while arguing, "I don't know everything in it. It was another city, a highway not a street, and I might be missing something about how roads work here. But if it's even partly true, you spend the money, you take the fig tree, and in a few years everyone's still sitting in traffic, except now there's no garden." He watched Bere's face do a small calculation, not about traffic, about votes.

"The garden doesn't move the commuter," Bere said. "That's the hard arithmetic."

Rosa arrived with a bag of tomatoes and set it on the table with a thud that aggrandized the gesture beyond what six pounds of fruit could justify, though Aiden suspected the effect was intentional. "Take these home," she told Bere. "Then tell your household the arithmetic while you eat something this soil made." Bere laughed, actually laughed, and took two, and signed nothing, and said he'd want the study emailed to him, which Aiden suspected was a polite exit but wrote down anyway on the back of a seed packet.

By afternoon the petition had nineteen signatures, one coffee ring, and the faint smell of tomato where the weights had been. Aiden pulled the rest of his weeds with more care, getting the roots, and thought about how the garden itself was an argument: cheap land, cheap food, a fig tree nobody had budgeted for, set against forty minutes of a stranger's evening, which he could not honestly say mattered less. He didn't know yet how the council would vote, or whether his one incisive fact would outlast a man's commute, or whether he had just aggrandized a difference of eleven lanes' worth of nothing.

Rosa came back with her empty watering cans. "He took the tomatoes," she said. "Aiden. He took the tomatoes."

He looked over at the fig tree, its leaves still holding the afternoon light, and started gathering the stones he'd finally found to weigh the petition down.

story:
Luca had come to Camp Abernathy for the sailing, and it was therefore a personal injustice that his favorite hour of the day was now the one spent in a basement lab with eleven other teenagers and forty laptops that smelled like warm dust.

"You signed up for Competitive Programming," said Priya, without looking up from her screen. "It's on your lanyard. It's practically tattooed on you."

"I signed up because my mother said I couldn't convalesce on a couch all summer. Her word. She looked it up so she could use it in the argument."

The project that week was to build a class in Java. Not just a program, a class, with private fields the outside world couldn't touch and getter methods standing politely at the door, and then to test it until it confessed everything. Luca had named his class Catalog, a thing that held a sorted array of item codes and answered whether a given code existed. Priya had named hers DragonHorde. "Because the fields are private," she said. "Like treasure. Nobody touches the hoard without a getter."

He liked that more than he wanted to admit. He'd been raised on his grandfather's cooking, all patient layering, nothing measured, and on his father's spreadsheets, where every cell was audited and every column had a rule. He'd never decided which way of thinking was his. The Catalog felt like both: a warm middle with a fence around it, and Luca sat there at his keyboard enjoying the impossible idea that he had invented a small, orderly country.

Then Friday came, and the competition dataset. Eight million item codes, sorted, waiting to be searched. The camp leaderboard, projected on the wall, ranked every team by speed. Luca's tests had all passed in the lab, small arrays, dozens of cases, green checkmarks like a lawn. He ran the big dataset and his program crashed with an error about a number that couldn't fit where he'd put it.

"That's not a speed problem," said Marcus from two seats over, leaning back in his chair with the serene confidence of a boy who had once eaten an entire lemon on a dare. "That's an arithmetic problem. Look at your midpoint line."

Luca looked. His binary search computed its middle as low plus high, then divided by two. On the test data it was fine. On the huge array, he was told, adding those two numbers could overflow, could go past what an int could hold, and the whole search came apart. Marcus pointed at the screen with a pencil. "Try low plus, in parentheses, high minus low, then divide by two. Same middle. No overflow."

Luca changed one line. The program ran the entire eight-million-code dataset and finished so fast the leaderboard had to blink twice to believe it. He spent the rest of the hour half triumphant, half annoyed, because the fix was small and the difference between his way and Marcus's way was a thing he hadn't known existed. He had trusted his tests, and his tests had trusted small numbers. It occurred to him that being right in the lab and being right in the world were two different jobs.

"You're doing the face," Priya said. She saved her file with a dramatic click. "The face of a boy discovering that the universe has fine print."

"Everyone thinks they're the main character until an int overflows," Luca said, and Marcus snorted so hard he knocked over his water bottle, which missed every laptop, a miracle the whole lab agreed to never report to the counselors.

The next morning, Saturday, was sailing, and Luca convalesced on the dock in the sun while the wind took a day off. Priya sat beside him with her laptop, which she had carried to the dock like a pet. "The autocrat has a bug," she announced. By the autocrat she meant the head counselor, Dennis, who had decreed that the leaderboard be wiped and the competition rerun that afternoon, since he refused to believe Luca's Catalog had beaten his favorite team. Dennis's rerun, it turned out, ran on an old machine in the boathouse, and Dennis's own sample search program, which he had written himself years ago and never once changed, crashed on the huge dataset in front of everyone.

"Let me guess his midpoint," Luca said.

"Low plus high, divided by two," said Priya, grinning. "Endemic. It's everywhere. Half the code on that machine has it."

Luca thought about walking up to Dennis and telling him about the one line. He thought about the two ways he knew of being in the world: his grandfather's, where you'd say nothing and quietly fix the man's soup, and his father's, where you'd present the audit in writing. He honestly did not know which was kinder, or which would work, or whether knowing the answer to an overflow question had anything to do with knowing the answer to a people question. He suspected it didn't. He suspected it might.

He ended up doing neither, exactly. He printed the fixed line on a scrap of paper, folded it once, and left it on the boathouse bench where Dennis kept his sunglasses. Then he went back to the dock.

Priya watched him do it and said nothing for a while. Then she said, "You know he's going to think it's a note from a secret admirer."

"It's a note from a secret admirer," Luca said. "I admire people who fix one line instead of arguing about the whole program."

Down the lake, a sail finally caught some wind, and a small orange boat tipped, righted itself, and kept going.

story:
The community centre on Ashbury Road smelled of floor wax and instant coffee, and on Thursday nights it belonged to the/mock trial club, which was really just eleven teenagers, a folding table, and a man named Mr. Okafor who had agreed to referee without ever explaining why. Aidan arrived early because he had drawn the worst possible assignment: arguing both sides of a school dress-code case before the mock Supreme Court. Not one side, then someone else's side. Both. In the same night, in front of people who would notice every contradiction.

"You'll argue for the student at seven and the school at seven forty," Mr. Okafor had told him, checking his watch as though the schedule were a legal document. "The case is about a girl suspended for wearing an armband to school, same as the old one. You'll need the famous line somewhere, or you'll lose on style points alone."

"What famous line?" Aidan had asked, and Mr. Okafor had only smiled, which Aidan found less mysterious than infuriating.

So he had spent the week in the library with a photocopied case brief, and on Tuesday night he had found it, reading it twice because the first time it had seemed too simple to be the thing everyone quoted. In Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969, the Supreme Court had ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate. He copied it onto an index card in careful print, then turned the card over and wrote the school's counter-argument on the back, and felt a small, absurd foreboding, as though the two sides of one card might start fighting in his jacket pocket.

At seven, standing at the folding table with the card face-down in front of him, Aidan argued for the student. He was clumsy at first, saying "um" like a metronome, but when he reached for the line, something shifted. "In Tinker v. Des Moines, in 1969, this Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." Priya, playing a justice, stopped doodling. Aidan kept going, and for ten minutes he was genuinely enraptured by his own argument, gesturing at nothing, imagining the schoolhouse gate, the armband, the girl standing outside both.

At seven forty he turned the card over.

"The school's position," he began, and heard his own voice flatten. The counter-argument was harder, and not only because he'd rehearsed it less. He argued that the armband disrupted class, that a school is not a street corner, and the justices leaned in anyway, because a hard argument well made is more interesting than an easy one shouted. But midway through, Priya asked him a question he hadn't prepared for: "Do you believe what you're saying right now?"

The room went quiet in the specific way rooms do when everyone has been thinking the same thing and is grateful someone else said it. Aidan looked at the card, at its two sides, and understood for the first time why Mr. Okafor had given him both. "I believe it's arguable," he said. "I believe the Court found for the students seven to two in 1969, and I believe the school still loses here, but I didn't understand why until I had to make the school's case and feel where it bends." He set the card down face-up, both halves visible. "The disruption argument isn't nothing. It's just not enough at the schoolhouse gate."

He'd expected laughter, or worse, the polite silence reserved for people who crack in public. Instead Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard, and DeShawn, playing the sternest justice, said, "That's the first honest answer anyone's given all night," and then ruined it by adding, "Counsel is still over time, though. By a lot."

Afterward, folding chairs stacked and the lights half off, Priya caught him at the door. "So which one are you actually?" she asked. "The kid with the armband or the school?"

Aidan held up the index card, both sides showing, edges soft from his grip. "Ask me again when it's real," he said, and put it in his pocket, where the two arguments sat together, unresolved, all the way home.

She liked the mornings at Lakeview Day Camp, the way the five-year-olds arrived with their backpacks still bobbing above their shoulders, the smell of sunscreen and cut grass outside the arts shed. She told her mother she was practically volunteering, since eight dollars an hour was hardly money at all. She did not mention that she had been keeping a tally in the back of her notebook since the first week, a column of hours with small sums beside it, because the tally was just for practice, the way one might practice budgeting.

In the third week of July, Deenie, who ran the oldest campers' group, wrenched her ankle on the dock steps and went home for the summer. The director, Ms. Amara, stood at the picnic table with her clipboard and asked who could cover Deenie's afternoons, the extended-care block that ran until six. Several hands went down again as fast as they had gone up. Violet raised hers and kept it there. By Friday she had worked the morning block, the afternoon block, and two extra days covering the front desk while the receptionist was out, and when she added the column in her notebook she counted fifty-one hours in one week.

She was not counting the money, she reminded herself. She was being useful, which was different. Rosa, her best friend at camp, had a theory about this. "You proselytize about not caring," Rosa said, peeling the label off her water bottle in one long strip. "You convert people to it. That's how much you care about not caring." Violet laughed and said Rosa should have been a lawyer, which was what Rosa's mother was and what Rosa was tired of hearing about.

The paycheck came on the second of August, a thin envelope with a stub inside. Violet read it in the supply closet where the extra life vests hung, because that was the only quiet place at two o'clock. The stub listed her regular hours at eight dollars. Then there was a second line, hours at twelve dollars an hour, eleven of them. Twelve was not a number she had earned anywhere. Eleven was a number she recognized, the amount past forty. She stood there doing arithmetic on the paint-spattered counter, and the total matched exactly, and she felt a small unearned glow, as though she had gotten away with something she had not even attempted.

She decided not to ask about it. If the camp wanted to overpay her, that was the camp's problem, and mentioning it might make someone realize a mistake and take the money back. She rehearsed several versions of this reasoning on the bus home and found all of them convincing. Rosa, when told, was less convinced. "You're being an apologist for your own greed," Rosa said, "and not even greed for money. Greed for being the girl who doesn't ask." Violet said that was the most convoluted compliment she had ever received, and also that Rosa should return the orange crayon she had borrowed in April.

But the twelve dollars sat in her mind the way a pulled thread sits in a sweater. On Monday she went to the office during nap block and found Ms. Amara laminating name tags. Violet put the stub on the desk, faceup, and tapped the second line. "I didn't work any senior hours," she said. "Why are eleven of my hours at twelve dollars?"

Ms. Amara looked at the stub, then at Violet, and something in her expression shifted, a loosening, as if she had been braced for a complaint and received a question instead. "That's not a mistake," she said. "It's the law. Non-exempt employees get one and a half times their regular rate for every hour past forty in a workweek. Eight times one and a half is twelve." She slid the stub back across the desk. "You crossed forty last week, so your last eleven hours paid at twelve. Most of your hours this summer won't, since you're usually under. But when you cover for someone, they can add up fast."

Violet said, mostly to the laminator, "I thought that was only for real jobs." Ms. Amara said the law did not distinguish, not in the way Violet meant, and turned the machine off between name tags. "Half the counselors never read their stubs," she added. "You read yours." She said it without particular praise, as a fact she had observed, and somehow that landed heavier than praise would have.

On the bus home, Violet took out her notebook and, next to her column of hours, wrote a second column, rate, and a third, earned, and filled them in for every week so far. The numbers were smaller than her old estimates, because her old estimates had quietly rounded up. She noticed this about herself and did not entirely know what to do with it, that her careful tally had been careful the way a funhouse mirror is careful. She was, she concluded, a person who liked to seem unconcerned with money while being extremely concerned with it, and she could admit that now without deciding yet whether to change it. Rosa would say this was progress. Rosa would also say the orange crayon thing again.

In August she signed up for two more of Deenie's afternoon blocks, telling Rosa it was for the experience. Rosa raised an eyebrow and said nothing sagacious, which in Rosa's mouth was practically a standing ovation. On the last Friday of the summer, Violet bought two ice creams with her own money from the truck by the lake, and handed one to Rosa, and said, "I'm only letting you think I'm generous. My hours past forty pay time and a half, and I checked the schedule." Rosa took the cone and bit the top off. "Fifty-one hours next week?" she asked, and Violet, watching the older campers tip their canoe in the shallows, said, "Fifty-two."

The scoreboard in left field had lost its middle digit, so the score read 4 instead of 14, and Victor thought that was as good a summary of the season as any. They were down five in the sixth. He stood in the on-deck circle twisting his bat when Danny Kohl, their third hitter, launched a double off the wall, and the whole dugout started hammering the bench like a drum line.

"That's three in a row for Kohl," Coach Renner said, mostly to himself, but loud enough. Victor heard him say to the assistant, "Get the ball to Kohl every time he's up. He's burning."

Victor was batting fourth. He had walked twice and singled once, and no one had hammered anything for him. When he came back to the bench after a groundout that moved Danny to third, Renner didn't look at him. He looked at Danny, who was spitting sunflower seeds into a paper cup and grinning.

"Next inning, if Kohl gets on, we bunt him over," Renner said. "Want Kohl swinging while he's hot."

"Coach, I'm four for seven the last two games," Victor said.

"And Kohl's hot tonight."

The word landed on Victor like a tag. Hot. As if Danny's body were a stove and the dial had been turned up by circumstance. Victor had read something once, late at night, phone light under his blanket because his roommate was asleep, a Wikipedia spiral that had started with coin flips. He tried to remember the details while he stood at second base in the top of the seventh, watching their left fielder take a bad route to a sinking line drive.

Between innings he found the page again, crouched by the bat rack. 1985. Three names: Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky. They had looked at basketball shooters and concluded that streaks were no more common than chance. There was a word for the belief, a word the study used, and Victor mouthed it to himself before he let anyone else hear it.

In the eighth they trailed by two. Danny led off with a walk, which did not portend anything, Victor told himself, though his hands were sweating anyway. Then Victor worked the count full and doubled into the left-center gap, and Danny scored. The dugout began hammering the bench again, and Victor, standing on second with his hands on his knees, realized they were hammering for him. For one turn of the order, he was the stove.

He led off the ninth with the score tied. On the third pitch he lined a single, and the first-base coach squeezed his shoulder. The next batter, a junior named Ellis, took three straight fastballs for strikes, and Victor stole second on the third one anyway, sliding in under the tag in a cloud of dust. When he stood and brushed himself off, Renner was signaling from the third-base box: bunt.

The idea was obvious. Ellis would make an out, Victor would take third, and Danny, three for four with the hot hand, would end it with one swing. The whole park could feel the plan assembling itself. Victor looked down at Danny in the on-deck circle, tapping his cleats with his bat, loose and happy and ready.

He called time and walked toward the third-base box.

"What are you doing," Renner said. Not a question.

"There was this study," Victor said. "Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky. They looked at basketball shooters, and the streaks weren't any more common than chance. They called it the hot hand fallacy."

Renner's jaw moved the way it did when he chewed gum that had gone to rubber. "This is baseball, not basketball."

"I know. I'm saying maybe Danny's not hot. Maybe he's just a good hitter who's had four balls fall in."

"Maybe you're a kid who read something on his phone."

"Coach," Danny called from the circle, easy, unbothered. "I'll take it from here."

Renner looked at Victor for a long second, then put the bunt sign back up, sharper this time, an obsolescent gesture now that every kid on the field could read the whole alphabet of signs. Victor went back to second. He thought about how his father described jury duty once, how the affidavit he'd signed felt heavier than the testimony itself, a thing you had to stand behind. Whatever happened next, he had said his page out loud, in front of everybody.

Ellis bunted. Victor took third. The left fielder's dead scoreboard digit hung above them all like a held breath. Danny dug in, twisted his hips once, and the first pitch came in low and outside.

"Take," the catcher said, and Victor, leading off third, watched the ball sail past and heard the crowd begin to rise.

The canoe tipped on the second day, and by the third morning the whole camp knew that Priya had been the one holding it crooked. Nobody said so out loud. They just let the fact drift around the mess hall like the smell of oatmeal, and Priya ate her toast with her shoulders up around her ears. Juliette, who had been paired with her for the Friday paddling assessment, understood that she had two weeks to solve a problem she could not name politely: her bow paddler was terrible, and she would have to say so, eventually, to her face.

Their counselor, a college junior named Dana who was working the summer between what she called "semesters of crisis," had been furloughed from her actual internship and seemed to regard canoe instruction as a form of hospice care for her career. She taught by shrugging. When Juliette asked how to tell a partner she was doing something wrong, Dana said, "Specifically. And like she's a person," and then went back to reading a battered social psychology textbook she kept folded open on the dock.

Juliette was not naturally a confronter. Her mother sold real estate and could parametrize any human interaction into a spreadsheet of outcomes; her father believed honesty was a virtue best practiced on other people's children. Juliette had absorbed both positions without committing to either, which meant she mostly said "it's fine" in a voice that made it clear it was not fine, which Priya had surely noticed.

The book on the dock turned out to matter. Juliette, drying her feet beside it while Priya retrieved a dropped paddle, read the page it happened to be open to. In 1999, two researchers, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, had found that people liked a partner more when that partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements. She read it twice, wondering whether Priya had been mirroring her all week, the copied laugh, the way she sat when Juliette sat, or whether it was the other way around and she was the copy.

"You're doing the thing," Priya said that evening, from the top bunk, in the dark.

"What thing."

"The mirror thing. There's a study. Some year in the nineties. Chartrand and Bargh. People like you more when you copy how they're sitting." A pause, then, more quietly: "Is that why you've been nice to me? Because you read the same page?"

Juliette lay still and considered lying, considered a hedonistic little fantasy in which she said yes and Priya laughed and the canoe became a boat that carried them both. "I read the page today," she said. "But I decided to pair with you before I read it. You don't have to believe that."

On Thursday, the last practice day, Priya put the canoe in the reeds twice. At lunch, out by the fire pit away from the others, Juliette made herself do it. "Your J-stroke is fine on flat water. The problem is when we turn, you switch sides a half second before I call it, so we're both on the same side and the boat walks into whatever's nearest. If you wait for the call, my steering can handle the rest." She heard her own voice, how specific it was, how it sounded almost like kindness, and how it was not quite kindness either, only information delivered at close range.

Priya turned her spork over in her hand. "You've been thinking about how to say that for days."

"Obviously."

"You could have just said I was bad."

"You're not bad. You're early." Priya almost smiled at that, and Juliette caught herself adjusting her posture to match the way Priya had drawn up one knee, and decided not to worry about which of them was doing the study and which was doing the finding. On Friday they came through the assessment channel upright, Priya waiting, with visible effort, for every call, and afterward she reached across the gunwale and splashed Juliette with the flat of her paddle. "Half a second," she said. "That's all I was borrowing."

story:
The group chat had forty-three unread messages by the time Naomi sat down at her kitchen table, and most of them were about Marcus. Someone had posted a screenshot of the school's new attendance system, which scanned faces in the hallway, and someone else had noticed that it had marked Marcus absent three days in a row, which was impossible, because Marcus was in her second period and had lent her a green highlighter only that morning. "The camera doesn't like me," Marcus had written, followed by the shrugging emoji, and then a wall of replies arguing about whether that was even possible.

Naomi typed, "It's a program. Programs don't like or dislike." She deleted it before sending. It sounded like something her father would say about the dishwasher.

"It's not that deep," Priya wrote. "So a computer glitches sometimes. Teachers make mistakes too."

"Yeah but teachers' mistakes are random," Marcus answered. "This thing's mistakes are all in one direction. Ask around. Who else is getting flagged?" Over the next hour, a pattern assembled itself out of scattered complaints: Marcus, who was Black; Ana, whose face the system seemed to read as male half the time; Jaylen, who wore a hoodie that flattened him into shadow. Not one of the flagged kids was white. Not one of them had thought to compare notes before.

Naomi scrolled back through the thread with her chin on her fist. In her civics class they had spent two weeks on the Constitution, and she had done her presentation on the Fourth Amendment, and she had felt virtuosic about it, standing at the front of the room with her index cards, laying out the logic of warrants and probable cause like a solved proof. She had not once, she realized now, connected any of it to the camera above the gym door.

Priya was still going. "Honestly who cares, I have nothing to hide. They can scan my boring face all day."

Naomi's thumbs hovered. She typed slowly. "Would you let me read your phone? Like all of it. Every text, every number you've called, how long you talked."

"That's different, you're a person."

"Okay, would you let a company you've never heard of read it?"

Priya sent the eye-roll emoji, but she didn't answer right away, and in the pause Theo jumped in with a link. "This actually happened," he wrote. "In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers."

"Not the calls?" Naomi asked, reading the article on her laptop while the chat blinked. "Just the records. Who you called and for how long."

"Millions of them," Theo confirmed. "Ordinary customers."

Priya came back online twenty minutes later. "Okay so I asked my mom and she said the government can't just do that, there are laws." Her next message took longer to appear, the typing indicator pulsing on and off. "But I looked it up and it happened anyway. So the laws and the doing are two different things."

Naomi leaned back and looked at the ceiling, which was her thinking posture, inherited from her mother. The scale of the leak felt tectonic to her, something enormous shifting beneath ordinary life without making a sound, and yet Priya's reaction had been a shrug until the shrugging got hard. Meanwhile the hallway camera was tiny, one bad system in one bad school, and it was ruining Marcus's attendance record in real time. Maybe that was the trick of it, she thought, that the enormous thing was easy to ignore and the small thing was fixable. She didn't type that. She wasn't sure it was true.

She opened a new message to Marcus directly. "Do you have the three absence emails?" He sent screenshots, timestamped, with the subject line ATTENDANCE ALERT in gray capitals. She forwarded them to the vice principal with a short paragraph asking whether the system had been tested across different skin tones, then copied the paragraph into the group chat so everyone could see what she'd asked and how. Theo immediately added that there were researchers who audited this kind of software professionally. Ana said her cousin had gotten a similar flag last year and nobody had believed her, and that seeing the pattern laid out in the thread made her feel less crazy, which was not a feeling Naomi had anticipated.

The vice principal replied the next morning: the vendor would be contacted, the flagged records held in suspense pending review, the attendance office instructed to accept manual corrections. It was not an apology and it was not a fix. Marcus reposted it with "small victories," and Priya, who had started the whole argument with "not that deep," wrote, "I still think most surveillance is boring people watching boring people. But I don't think the boring people all get watched the same."

Naomi read that twice. She wanted to tell Priya that she had just stated the entire problem in one sentence, but she suspected that saying so would make Priya retreat. Instead she wrote, "Meeting before school Monday, room 114, we're drafting what we want them to change. Bring the screenshots."

Twelve people clicked the little thumbs-up, including Marcus, including Ana, including Priya, last of all, at 11:42 that night.

Morgan had opened the coffee shop at five, and by seven the morning light was coming through the front windows in long stripes across the counter, catching the steam off the espresso machine so that the whole room looked faintly theatrical. Her phone sat face down beside the register, but she had already seen the message that morning, before the alarm even finished: a photograph from her aunt Meera in Bangalore, holding up one finger stained a deep, unapologetic purple. Beneath it, in her aunt's brisk style, no greeting, no punctuation: "voted. no one can vote twice. they mark us with silver nitrate ink. since the 1962 general election. always indelible."

The customers that morning were divided into two camps, which Morgan found funny in a distant way, since the election itself seemed to divide everyone into the same two camps. There were the people who ordered quickly and left quickly, wearing their seriousness like a coat, and there were the people who lingered and wanted to talk. A man in a rain jacket, waiting on a cortado, told her he had voted at six a.m. because delay was deleterious to resolve; he said it smiling, but he meant it. Morgan was an epicure of the slow morning herself, and she liked him anyway.

Her father had called the night before while she was closing out the register. His position was arithmetic: you vote for the candidate who can actually win, because a vote is not a diary entry, it is an instrument, and you do not use a fine instrument to make yourself feel interesting. Her roommate Jules held the opposite conviction and did not merely hold it but proselytized, in the kitchen, on the stairs, over the last of the yogurt: that a vote spent on the lesser evil was still spent on evil, and the only honest ballot was the one that could embarrass you at dinner. Morgan had listened to both of them with the sensation of holding two magnets the wrong way around.

Between orders she turned her aunt's photograph over in her mind. Meera was seventy-one and had stood in a queue since before dawn, and she was proud of the stain on her finger, proud enough to send it across an ocean to a niece she'd met three times. Morgan kept thinking that the ink made something visible that her own ballot would not. In this country her vote would leave no mark on her at all; she would walk out of the gymnasium looking exactly like a person who had not voted, and no one, including herself, would be able to tell the difference afterward.

At two o'clock her shift ended and Jules came in, ordered a large coffee with an excess of ceremony, and slid into the chair opposite Morgan's spot at the corner table. "You're going at five, right?" Jules said. "Polls close at seven. I already went. I voted my conscience and I have never felt so clean, except morally I mean, I still haven't showered." Morgan laughed and wrapped her hands around her cup. She laid out the two arguments the way she laid out the pastry case in the morning, each item in its place, and found that neither of them, laid out side by side, actually canceled the other. Her father was right that a vote was an instrument. Jules was right that instruments were all anyone ever hid behind. What Morgan settled on, slowly, watching a busker outside tune a guitar badly, was a position with a splinter in it: she would vote for the winnable candidate she distrusted less, and she would not pretend the splinter wasn't there.

"You're sure?" Jules said. "Because if you're not, the clean thing is right there."

"I'm not sure," Morgan said. "I'm decided. It's a different thing."

At the gymnasium the line moved in a shuffle, past folding tables, past a woman with a clipboard who found Morgan's name and pronounced it correctly, which almost nobody did. The ballot was longer than she had expected, full of judges and school board members and a referendum about storm drains, and she stood in the booth longer than she meant to, reading everything twice. When she finally fed the sheet into the scanner, it made a sound like a printer accepting its fate, and a poll worker peeled a sticker off a roll and handed it over with the solemnity of a medal.

Outside, in the long light, she took a photograph of her own hand, sticker stuck to one finger, and sent it to Meera with the caption "mine." Then, because her pen had leaked on the walk over, there was a small blue smudge along the side of her index finger, and she photographed that too and sent it as well, holding the finger up exactly the way her aunt had. The reply came while she was still standing on the corner: "very good. but yours washes off. vote harder next time."

story:
Parker arrived at the mall eleven minutes early, which he decided was six minutes too many, so he walked twice around the fountain near the east entrance and then stood where he could see both escalators. Marisol had said two o'clock by the pretzel stand, and it was 1:54. A rope and a line of plastic plants delimit the seating area there, and he stood just outside it, holding the second button of his shirt closed between two fingers, a habit he had not noticed until his brother pointed it out in a scathing text that morning: "Unbutton the collar, you look like you're being buried in it."

They had met at a party neither of them wanted to be at, in a kitchen, where she had argued that the movie everyone loved was actually badly paced and he had agreed too quickly and then, correcting himself, argued the opposite until she laughed. Now she came down the escalator with her hands in her jacket pockets, and he took his hand off the button.

"I was thinking bowling," she said. "There's lanes in the basement level."

The bowling alley was loud in a way that made talking easier, because nothing either of them said was required to be important. She bowled straight and fast; he bowled with a strange three-step approach he'd invented at a birthday party in seventh grade and never fixed. Through two games they were close enough that the machine put them into a tiebreaker frame, and in that frame she threw three strikes in a row, arms up, spinning to face him with her chin out, and he got the last two he needed by a margin of four pins.

His heart was going hard enough that he could feel it in his ears. She sat down next to him on the bench, still warm from the game, still grinning, and said, "You want to know a gross fact about this exact moment?"

"Always."

"Okay, so. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal." She picked up a napkin and folded it into a smaller square. "It's when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby."

"Where did you read that?"

"Psych class. There's a study where they had guys cross a scary bridge and meet a woman on the other side, and way more of them called her afterward than the guys on the boring bridge." She set the napkin down. "So I don't trust anything I feel in the ten minutes after a tiebreaker."

He laughed, and then did not, because he had been about to say something and the fact arrived in front of it like a car pulling out. All evening, under the arcade's strobing lights and the noise of the lanes, he had been reading his own pulse as evidence about her, and it might have been, and it might have been the escalators and the tiebreaker and the fact that he had rehearsed this date out loud in his car.

"So what do you do," he said, "if you can't tell the difference?"

"You wait for a boring minute. And then you see what's still there."

They left the bowling alley and drifted past a travel agency with a wall-sized photo of a fjord, a sheer black wall of rock dropping into still water, with a single white ferry making a wake across it. Marisol stopped. "My grandmother grew up on one of those. She says Americans photograph them because we don't have anything that old and quiet."

"We have malls," Parker said, and she laughed in the exact way she had in the kitchen, quick and then covered, like she was rationing it.

They walked the length of the second floor, past the phone cases and the candle store, and he noticed that his heart had gone back to its normal work and that the quiet it left was not empty. He still wanted to sit near her. He also understood, honestly, that wanting something in a quiet minute and wanting it in a loud one were different tests, and that he had only passed one of them so far, and that she might be running the same experiment on him.

At the fountain they stopped without deciding to. The coins on the bottom had gone green except one, near the center, that was still bright.

"Boring minute," Marisol said, checking her phone. "It's 4:12. Nothing is happening."

"Right," he said. "Nothing."

She put the phone away and looked at the water. He looked at it too. Then she said, "I get frozen yogurt with people I don't like. Just so the data's clean."

"Is that an offer?"

"It's a methodology," she said, and started walking toward the food court without checking whether he followed.

story:
Nicole had circled the psychology building twice before going in, because the boy handing out maps had a clipboard and a lanyard and the confident posture of someone who intended to eviscerate her with friendliness if she gave him the chance. Inside, the hallway smelled like floor wax and cut fruit from the welcome table. A banner read DISCOVER YOUR FUTURE, which seemed like a lot to ask of a folding table and a bowl of orange slices.

She was here for one reason: the department had a research lab that studied adolescent decision-making, and Nicole had spent most of senior year convinced that decisions were the only currency she had. Which college, which major, which city, whether to say yes to Danny Merck before graduation or after, whether after even meant anything. Her mother said she overthought. Her mother said this while weighing two brands of olive oil for ten minutes at the grocery store, so Nicole took it as a compliment.

The lab table was staffed by a graduate student named Priya, who wanted, visibly and urgently, for someone, anyone, to sign the interest sheet, because the department chair counted signatures and Priya had exactly four. "You can put your email," Priya said, sliding the clipboard closer before Nicole had spoken. "There's no commitment. It's just interest. Hypothetical interest is also fine."

"Tell me about the research first," Nicole said.

"Self-control," Priya said. "How people choose between something now and something later. We run versions of the delay task with adolescents."

Nicole's mother appeared beside her, holding a coffee she had not paid for, from a table marked FOR ADMITTED STUDENTS ONLY. "Oh, the marshmallow study," her mother said. "I know that one."

"You do not," Nicole said.

"I do. They gave little kids one marshmallow and told them if they didn't eat it, they'd get a second one later. A 1990 follow-up of those preschoolers found the kids who waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers." Her mother sipped the stolen coffee, pleased with herself. "You would have eaten it immediately. You ate a whole birthday cake at four. I have photographs."

A father hovering nearby with his own prospective student laughed. "So one afternoon with a marshmallow decides your whole life," he said. "Great. My son waited an hour once for a video game and now he can't wait five minutes for anything."

The son, arms crossed, said, "That's not what it means."

"It tends," Priya said carefully, glancing at the chair's office down the hall. "It's a tendency. Not a destiny." She rotated the clipboard so the blank lines faced them all.

Nicole looked at the sheet. She thought of Danny, who wanted an answer before September, and of the gap between the two of them, which was mostly a gap between how they each thought about later. He thought later was a place you arrived at by accident. She thought later was a place you built on purpose, brick by tedious brick, and she had always privately considered this a moral distinction, hers the altruistic one, his the selfish. She was starting to suspect that was unfair. He was generous in the present, actually, in ways she never was because she was too busy preparing for the future. Two temperaments, not two ethics. The marshmallow kids weren't better children. They were just children whose waiting happened to be measured.

Still. The study tracked something real, or the numbers wouldn't have moved. A tendency was a counterpoint to a destiny, not a refutation of it, and Nicole could hold both at once without pretending either one was the whole song.

"I'm not saying it's destiny," the father was saying to his son, in the tone of a man saying it was destiny.

"I'll sign," Nicole said. She wrote her name, then her email, then, after a pause, her phone number, which was more than the form asked for. Priya beamed as though Nicole had donated an organ.

"That's five," Priya whispered, mostly to herself.

Her mother linked arms with her as they walked out past the orange slices and the banner. "So did you learn your future?"

"I learned that a four-year-old with a birthday cake doesn't decide anything," Nicole said. "And that I still would have eaten it."

Outside, the map boy had abandoned his post and was giving directions to a lost family anyway, pointing with his whole arm, unbothered by the fact that he was pointing the wrong way.

story:
Sebastian had promised his geography teacher a map by Monday, and by Saturday afternoon the promise had begun to smell like a trap. He sat at the kitchen table with his mother's laptop, a trial version of a geographic information system blinking at him like it was daring him to touch it. The assignment was to overlay flood risk and housing on a map of their own city, and the software seemed to think that "overlay" meant "crash." He clicked a layer, clicked another, and watched the whole river vanish from the screen.

"You've killed the river," said his little sister Priya from the counter, where she was theoretically making toast. "RIP river."

"It's not dead, it's hidden. There's a difference." He right-clicked everything he could find. Somewhere under all these menus, he knew, the floodplain was still there, patient as a cat under a blanket. The trouble was that the software wanted everything codified first: which layer on top, which colors meant what, which shapes counted as housing and which were just sheds the city had never bothered to label. It refused to guess. It was, he decided, the most stubborn thing in the house, and Priya was sitting right there.

She came over anyway, toast in hand, and dropped a worksheet next to his laptop. "You're good at maps. Look at this and tell me it's not a triangle wearing a hat."

It was a population pyramid for Niger, and she was right, it barely looked like a pyramid at all. The bars were widest at the very bottom, stacked with children, narrowing so steeply toward the top that the whole thing resembled a triangle balanced on its tip. Next to it sat Japan's pyramid, which bulged in the middle like a wasp that had swallowed a marble. "We have to write what the shape means," Priya said. "For schools, I think. But I don't get why it matters."

Sebastian almost said the first thing that came into his head, which was that Niger had one of the highest birth rates in the world, so of course the base was wide and children made up a huge share of the people. Then he stopped, because the same thought had bent back toward his own map. On his screen, if he ever got the layers to agree, the floodplain ran through the cheapest parts of the city. Cheap housing, lots of families, lots of kids. The two shapes were talking to each other across the table, and he was the only one who could hear it.

"Look," he said, turning the laptop so she could see. He had finally found the layer panel, buried like treasure, and the river was back, a blue vein stitched through the city. He toggled on the flood risk layer and a pale wash of green spread over the south side. Then he added housing, and little squares clustered thick inside the green, like moss growing on the dangerous part of a rock. "That's where the water goes if it floods. And that's where the houses are. Same place."

Priya chewed her toast. "So that's bad."

"It's worse than bad, it's boring," Sebastian said. "Everybody already knows poor people live by the river. The map just says it in green." He sat back, annoyed at his own map, which had taken all afternoon to state the obvious. Then he tapped her worksheet. "But look at your triangle again. All those kids at the bottom. Where do you put schools for that many kids? And now look at my map. Where are the schools?" He pulled up another layer, the one he'd originally thought was useless, and the schools appeared as small orange dots. There were almost none inside the green.

For a while neither of them said anything, which for Priya was a geological event. "So the most kids," she said slowly, "are in the places with the most water and the least schools."

"That's the map I want to make," Sebastian said. He was already dragging layers, stacking them in an order that made a kind of argument: flood risk under housing under schools, each one thin enough to see through, so the whole picture came out like a photograph developed in stages. The software, mollated by correct syntax, finally rendered it without complaint. The south side of the city glowed like a bruise.

He knew, in an honest corner of his mind, that he still wasn't sure what the map proved. Maybe the school data was old. Maybe the flood model was cautious or wild. He couldn't tell from a green wash whether a hundred-year storm meant anything to a kid walking to school in ordinary rain. Those doubts he wrote in small letters at the bottom of the screen, the way you'd confess something in a footnote.

Priya leaned in and read his caption. Then she picked up her worksheet, wrote two sentences about wide bases and classrooms, and pointed her pencil at his screen. "So what you're saying is, your flood map and my triangle pyramid should get married."

"It's not a marriage," Sebastian said. "It's more of a rapprochement." He paused. "Two things that weren't talking to each other, sitting down at the same table."

"Like you and that software all afternoon," Priya said, and stole the last of his toast.

story:
Sierra set the spaghetti pot on the trivet and stood behind her chair instead of sitting in it, which was how her family knew something was coming. Her mother ladled sauce for her little brother without looking up. Her father was already halfway through the bread.

"I need to say something about the thing with Priya," Sierra said. "The rumor about her cheating on the calc final. Everyone's saying I started it, and I kind of did, but I didn't know it wasn't true when I said it."

Her brother paused with his fork in the air, delighted. Her mother put down the ladle.

Two weeks before, in the parking lot after sixth period, Sierra had told two girls from her study group that Priya had been seen with the answer key, which was what a boy named Dominic had told her. She had believed it completely, mostly because Dominic had a way of telling things that made doubting him feel rude. By Friday, half the junior class had heard a version in which Priya had a stolen copy of the exam, and by Monday the vice principal had called Priya's parents, and Priya had stopped eating lunch in the cafeteria.

"All I said was that I heard it," Sierra went on, sitting down at last. "That's what I keep telling myself. I heard it, and I passed it on, and I didn't check it with anyone, not even Priya. I just assumed it was out there already."

"Was it out there?" her father asked, which was the question she had spent the drive home dreading, because she had finally checked today, and it wasn't. Dominic had made it up, or stretched something small into something ruinous, and when she'd cornered him by the gym he'd shrugged and said he was joking, that she should have known that.

Her mother reached over and refilled her water glass even though it was nearly full, a thing she did when she wanted a person to have something to hold. "You know we're not going to fix this by figuring out exactly how guilty you are," she said. "You were there, so you were part of it. That part isn't complicated."

"It feels complicated, though," Sierra said. She pulled out her phone and opened her ethics notes, the ones she'd reread during seventh period instead of doing her lab. "We covered Aristotle like a month ago, before any of this happened, and I took the stupidest notes, and now it's all I can think about. He held that people are responsible for what they do voluntarily," she read, "and that things done under force, or through ignorance of the circumstances, can be involuntary."

Her brother made a face. "So you're off the hook because you were ignorant?"

"No, that's the part I keep going back and forth on. I didn't know the circumstances. I didn't know it was false, and I didn't know I was the only source, because I thought I was repeating something. But Aristotle's not giving out a prize for ignorance, he's drawing a line. The question is where the line falls." She turned the phone off and pushed her fork through the pasta. "And ignorance of the circumstances isn't the same as not bothering to look at them. I could have asked Priya one question. I could have asked Dominic where he got it. That's not force, and it's not really ignorance either. It's more like I was fine not knowing."

Her father had stopped eating. "What are you going to do," he said, and it came out as a statement, not a demand, which somehow made it heavier.

"Tomorrow I'm going to the vice principal and telling him exactly where it started, and then I'm going to tell Priya the same thing, to her face, and ask her what she wants me to do about it, since I'm the one who made it loud. I can't undo it, but I can stop letting the blame land on her for being upset about it." She swallowed. "I'm not going to try to talk Dominic into confessing. I considered it, honestly, I had this whole plan to cajole him into going with me, make it seem like we'd both look better. But that's me managing my share again instead of just carrying it."

"The apportionment of blame," her mother said, half smiling, using the word from the ethics unit too, the one the class had bandied about for a week. "You always did like to divide things fairly, even when you were six, splitting Halloween candy into exact piles."

"I liked it better then," Sierra said, and for the first time all dinner, her brother laughed, and she let herself laugh a little too, because the alternative was crying into the sauce.

Later, while she dried the dishes her mother washed, she was less sanguine than she'd sounded at the table. She kept seeing Priya in the library today, head down over a textbook, and she had walked past her twice without speaking, both times, and that was done voluntarily, with full knowledge of the circumstances, and no philosopher could grade it otherwise. On Monday she would say everything she'd planned. Tonight there was still a text she owed, and her thumb hovered over Priya's name for a long moment before she set the phone face-down on the counter and picked up the last wet plate.

Ryder clocked in at four and found the new cameras already mounted above the self-checkout lanes, four black domes like the top halves of eggs. Marisol, the shift lead, was taping a sign to the kiosk that said, in corporate sans-serif, "This area is monitored for quality assurance." She smoothed the tape with her thumb and did not look at him.

"Every lane?" Ryder asked.

"Every lane, the break room, the loading dock." She handed him the tape gun. "Loss prevention says the old system missed things. The new one flags suspicious behavior automatically." She said "automatically" the way people say a word they've just learned from a memo.

The system flagged its first customer within the hour. Mrs. Okonkwo, who came in every Tuesday for cat food and half a watermelon, set her reusable bag on the scale without scanning it, and the kiosk froze itself and asked her, in a pleasant chime, to wait for assistance. Ryder knew her bag. She'd been carrying that bag since before he worked here, and she put it on the scale because the floor was wet near the registers and she didn't want the canvas soaked. He keyed in his code and the lane unlocked. When she'd gone, the tablet in the back room showed him a report: the system had tagged her as "high risk, repeat pattern." It had flagged her the previous Tuesday too, and the one before, and no one had told her.

At the register he explained the bag, the wet floor, all of it, typing into a form with a box labeled "operator override, reason required." The form didn't have a box for "the machine is wrong about people." He typed "customer known to staff, no intent," and submitted it, and wondered who read those, if anyone.

The second flag came an hour later, and it was Dev, the college kid who worked weekends and stole, mildly and openly, a bag of chips most Saturdays, which everyone knew and no one cared about because Dev was nineteen and hungry and the store threw out unsold chips by the case. The system had never once flagged Dev, because Dev scanned everything and paid for his chips and ate the ones from the damaged shelf that were already written off. The machine couldn't see the difference between a woman putting a bag on a scale and a kid taking what the store had already abandoned. It could only see what it had been told to see.

Ryder had a philosophy elective in the fall, his first semester, and the syllabus had come in the mail that week. Thursday's reading was a book called Discipline and Punish, by a man named Foucault, published in 1975. He'd skimmed the assigned pages on his phone during break, mostly not understanding them, until he hit a section about a building designed by a man named Bentham: a prison arranged in a circle so that one watcher in the center could see into every cell, and, more importantly, the prisoners could never tell whether they were being watched at any given moment. Foucault had used it as a metaphor, the book said, for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation. Ryder read that sentence twice in the break room, under a camera dome with a blinking green light.

He showed the page to Marisol on her break, holding the phone out over the hash browns she was eating cold from the container.

"Sounds like this place," she said.

"It's called a panopticon," Ryder said. "Bentham's building." He almost added something about the metaphor, about institutions, but he stopped, because Marisol was looking up at the dome above them and he wanted to see what she saw first.

"I don't mind being watched," she said slowly. "I mind being sorted. Watched, fine, my grandmother watched everybody from her porch and it kept the block safe. But the machine doesn't watch. It decides, and then somebody believes it." She scraped the last of her hash browns. "Mrs. Okonkwo gets flagged three weeks in a row, that's a record now. Dev never gets flagged, so Dev's clean. That's the pernicious part, right? Not the cameras. The filing."

Ryder thought about arguing that the cameras and the filing were the same thing, that the whole design of it was what Foucault meant, that even the customers performing their innocence at the kiosk, holding every item up like an offering, were already changed by the possibility of the lens. But Marisol was also right that a porch and a watchtower weren't the same, that her grandmother's watching had mercy built into it, an actual face you could turn toward and explain about your wet bag and your cat food. He couldn't get the two ideas to sit still together. Maybe the watchtower was just a porch with no grandmother in it. Maybe that was the whole difference.

At closing he ran the override report one more time, the way he'd started doing, printing the flags for customers he knew and stapling his explanations to them. There were eleven pages. He put them in Marisol's locker with a note that said "for the district meeting, if you want them." Then he went back out to the lanes, where the domes blinked green in the dark, and Mrs. Okonkwo's Tuesday bag was hanging on the hook by register three where she'd left it, so she wouldn't have to carry it home and back.

He took it down and folded it and put it behind the counter where it would stay dry.

"See you Tuesday," he said to the empty lane, and clocked out.

Alexa had the roast out of the fridge and salted before her father came into the kitchen, still in his work clothes, still carrying the argument from last night in the set of his shoulders. The dinner was for her grandmother's birthday, and her grandmother was arriving at seven, which gave Alexa four hours, no more, no less, because a roast this size wanted three and a half in the oven and she refused to serve it late.

"You're doing it the way she does it," her father said, reading the recipe card over her shoulder. Its corners were soft with age and its handwriting was her grandmother's, a cramped, elegant script that seemed to codify every lesson the woman had ever learned about Sunday dinners into one index card. Rest until internal temperature reaches 160. Serve.

"I'm doing it exactly the way she does it," Alexa said. "That's the whole point."

He grunted and went to change, and Alexa slid the roast into the oven and set the thermometer probe through the side, the way a video had shown her, deep into the center of the meat. She had told her father she wanted to make this dinner because she wanted to prove something, though she hadn't said what, and he hadn't asked. Proving something to an intransigent man was, her mother liked to say, a hobby with poor compensation. Her mother also said everything happens for a reason, which Alexa considered a bromide, the kind of statement that closed a conversation rather than opened one.

At 4:40 the thermometer read 158, and by 5:05 it touched 160, and Alexa pulled the roast out, triumphant, and tented it in foil exactly as the card instructed, and went upstairs to change out of her flour-dusted shirt. When she came down twenty minutes later and sliced into it, the center had gone from pink to the dull brown-gray of overcooked meat, all the way to the edges, as though the roast had kept cooking on the counter while her back was turned. Which, she realized, standing there with the knife in her hand, it had.

She called Dani, whose family did competition barbecue, and got the words she needed in one sentence. "Carryover cooking," Dani said. "It keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a big roast like that can go up by several degrees while it rests." Alexa sat down on the kitchen floor with the phone against her ear and the recipe card in her lap and did the arithmetic she should have done hours ago. If it climbed that far during the rest, then her grandmother, cooking on a stove in 1974 with no probe thermometer, had been pulling hers off the heat early all along, and never knew the numbers behind what her hands had learned. The card said 160, and the card meant the finished temperature, not the pulling temperature, and there was a difference, and Alexa had followed the letter of it straight into a well-done roast.

"There's no time for another one," her father said from the doorway. He had seen the sliced meat. It was 5:35. The butcher was fifteen minutes away, closing at six, and the only roasts left would be smaller ones, and a smaller roast would cook in time but not by the card, not by any card, because the card assumed the big cut her grandmother always bought.

"Do we tell her?" Alexa asked.

Her father looked at the ruined roast for a long moment, the man who had insisted last night that some things shouldn't be modernized, that the old ways carried knowledge the new ones couldn't see. "We don't tell her," he said. "We start over. And you," and here he paused, visibly revising something in himself, "pull it early. Don't wait for the card."

They drove to the butcher with the radio off, Alexa navigating on her phone, and got the last shoulder roast, barely half the size of the first. Back in the kitchen they worked side by side, her father rough-chopping the vegetables he'd refused to touch earlier, Alexa salting the new meat, and it went into the oven at 5:55 with the probe set and a target in her head that was not the number on the card. She watched the thermometer like a hawk and, when it read several degrees below what the card demanded, she stood with her hand on the oven door and felt the full weight of trusting a number she had never trusted before.

At 6:58 she pulled it, tented it, and did not go upstairs. She stood at the counter and watched the thermometer climb through the rest, degree by degree, arriving almost exactly where her grandmother's card had said the meat should finish. When the doorbell rang, Alexa was already slicing, and the center came up rosy and correct. Her grandmother came into the kitchen still unbuttoning her coat, and her father put a plate in front of her without a word of explanation, and the old woman looked at the pink center, then at Alexa, then at the thermometer still lying beside the carving board.

"You used a probe," her grandmother said.

"I used your card too," Alexa said, and set the first slice on her grandmother's plate.

The garage smelled of cut grass and old gasoline, and the dust that came through the window slats moved so slowly it seemed to coagulate in the light before settling. Savannah sat on an overturned milk crate with her grandfather's guitar across her knees, a nylon-stringed thing with a crack along the body that made certain notes buzz like a wasp in a jar. She had been working on the same four chords for eleven days. Her fingertips had gone past sore into something numb and tender at once, like sunburn healing.

Devon came through the side door without knocking, the way he had since they were nine. He set his bike helmet on the workbench, watched her fingers stumble from C to G, and winced.

"Still on that?"

"Sixty hours down," she said. "I've been counting."

"That's the problem, though." He picked up a lug nut from a coffee can and rolled it between his palms. "You know the ten-thousand-hour rule, right? Malcolm Gladwell. He wrote that book in 2008, Outliers, the one everybody's uncle quotes. Ten thousand hours to get good at anything. My cousin read it and gave up chess over it." He tossed the lug nut back into the can. "You're starting guitar at seventeen, Sav. Do the math. That's pointless numbers of hours. You'd be thirty before you're even decent."

She let the chord ring until it died. "You finished that book?"

"I read enough of it."

Outside, past the half-open door, the creek at the back of the lot ran low for August, its riparian edge showing as a strip of cracked mud and bent sedges where the water used to be. Her grandfather had built this garage facing the water on purpose, she'd always supposed, the way he did most things on purpose.

That night she looked it up on her laptop at the kitchen table while her mother washed lettuce at the sink. Gladwell, 2008, the number ten thousand, the word outliers. She scrolled past summaries and listicles until she found the twist: the researcher whose work the book leaned on, a man named Ericsson, had said afterward that the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Not ten thousand, not any number. Quality. She read the sentence twice, then closed the laptop and sat listening to the water running over the lettuce.

The next morning she tried an experiment. Instead of playing the four chords for an hour while half listening to the radio, she gave herself fifteen minutes and one rule: every change from C to G had to be slow enough that she could watch her own fingers move and see, before it happened, exactly where they would land. She missed the change nine times out of ten at first. Then seven. By the third day of this she could do it without looking, and the surprise of it, the clean landing, made her laugh out loud alone in the garage.

Devon came by Thursday. He brought two sodas and a grievance about his summer reading, and he watched her run the changes again with the radio off.

"Your chords sound better," he admitted. "Weird. You practicing more?"

"Less, actually."

"That doesn't even make sense."

She kept playing while she explained, half because it was easier to say hard things with her hands busy. "So Gladwell's the one who made the rule famous, right? Ten thousand hours, in Outliers, 2008. But Ericsson, the guy whose research it came from, he said later it's the quality of the practice that matters more than any fixed number of hours. Not that hours mean nothing. Just that the number isn't the thing." She flubbed a change, backed up, tried it slow. "I don't know if I'm proving him right or if I just had a good week. That part I can't tell yet."

Devon drank his soda and thought about it the way he thought about most things, chewing the inside of his cheek. "So it's not a rule, it's more like a rumor about a rule."

"That's one way to put it."

"And you're still going to be bad for a long time either way."

"Probably years." She said it without flinching and found that she meant it, which was its own strange relief. Devon was, at bottom, a pragmatist; he wanted to know what a plan cost and what it paid. She understood that, and she also understood that he had mistaken the question. She wasn't trying to arrive somewhere. She wanted the thing itself, the buzz-cracked D chord and the slow landing, today, at hour sixty or sixty thousand.

Whether quality really outweighed the count, she couldn't yet say from the inside of her own sixty hours. Maybe both were true at once and the tension between them never resolved; she could hold that. She set the guitar down, and they walked out past the workbench to look at the creek, its water so shallow and clear they could count the pebbles on the bottom.

"Show me the slow thing," Devon said. "The watching your fingers thing."

She went back in, picked up the guitar, and placed his hand on the neck beside hers.
