story:
The sign on the door of Ferrand Market said CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE, and beneath it, in the manager's careful handwriting, a second sheet: THIS IS A LOCKOUT. PLEASE DO NOT ATTEMPT TO ENTER. Autumn read it twice, then checked her phone against the time, as though the numbers might reconcile themselves. Her shift started at four. It was ten past. Through the glass she could see the registers dark and Mr. Okonkwo from produce standing in the aisle with his coat already on, not shopping, not working, just standing there like furniture that had been arranged by someone in a hurry.

She found the union hall by asking Mr. Okonkwo, who came out a side door when she knocked on it. It was a low brick building three blocks over, between a dentist and a shuttered laundromat, with folding chairs in rows and a coffee urn that had clearly been running since morning. A man at a card table was copying names into a ledger. When she gave her name he paused over it, said, "New hire, September," and wrote her in anyway, in a column that had its own heading.

She had assumed, walking over, that this was a strike. That was the word from the news, the word with the picket lines and the drums. But the man at the table, whose lanyard said DENNIS, told her the workers hadn't refused to come in. "The company shut us out," he said. "They changed the locks Friday night. That's the difference, and it matters. In a strike, we'd be refusing to work. This way, they're refusing to let us." A woman beside him added, "They call it a lockout," and went back to her clipboard, as if the word itself were the whole argument.

Autumn took a chair near the back and tried to fit the pieces together the way she would a proof. Her calculus teacher called the small stepping-stone propositions lemmas: things you had to establish first before the main claim would stand. This was one of those, she thought. Who stopped the work determined what everything downstream meant: whether the stoppage was a weapon of the workers or of the employer, who was supposed to feel the pressure, whose patience was being spent. She had worked at Ferrand for six weeks, two of them in training. She was, she realized, the most junior person in the room by a margin of about nine years.

Ms. Ferreira, the assistant manager, found her there within the hour. She came in through the dentists' shared door, still wearing her lanyard, and sat down beside Autumn without being invited. "I'm not management," she said first, which was the kind of sentence that made Autumn listen harder. "I'm hourly, same as you. But they've asked me to call the part-timers, in order of hire date, and offer them the shifts. The store reopens Monday with whoever comes." She said it flatly, reading the room while pretending to read her phone. What she wanted was visible in her hands: she wanted Autumn to say yes so that Ms. Ferreira could tell the district office she had tried, so that her own name would appear on the list of people who had tried. "You'd keep your wages," she added. "Time and a half on Sunday, if it goes long."

The wages were the same wages the locked-out people in the folding chairs had. That was the thing Autumn kept circling back to. Dennis had a handout, photocopied crookedly, with the current contract language on one side and the company's proposed language on the other: the Sunday premium replaced with a flat rate, the scheduling notice cut from two weeks to one, a clause about "operational flexibility" that seemed, to Autumn's inchoate understanding of contracts, to mean that flexibility flowed entirely one direction. She read it twice. It was not about any single line. It was about who decided.

"I almost went in," she admitted later, to a woman named Priya who stocked dairy and had appointed herself in charge of the picket schedule, a grid on butcher paper so new the marker still smelled. "This morning I thought the doors were just stuck." It wasn't quite the truth, and Priya seemed to know it, because she raised one eyebrow and waited. The truth was that Autumn had stood outside for a full minute thinking about time and a half, and that standing here now felt like a way to expiate the minute, and that expiation was probably the wrong reason to do anything, the way guilt was a bad reason to vote.

The twist came at the Thursday meeting, and it arrived through Mr. Okonkwo, quiet Mr. Okonkwo of produce, who stood up when Dennis called for new business and said he had something to disclose. He had been in the building Friday night when the locks were changed. He had helped the locksmith carry his tools in, because the man had his hands full and it seemed like courtesy, and only afterward understood what he had carried them toward. He told the room this in a voice that kept dropping. Somebody near the front started to laugh, couldn't decide whether it was that kind of story, and stopped.

Autumn watched Dennis decide, in real time, what to do with a confession like that. He didn't absolve him and he didn't shame him. He wrote something in the ledger, then crossed it out, then said, "Saturday, you're on the six a.m. picket, and you're bringing the coffee." Mr. Okonkwo nodded like a man being sentenced, and half the room laughed for real this time, and Priya wrote his name at the top of the grid in letters bigger than anyone else's.

Saturday at six it was dark and very cold. Autumn held a sign she hadn't expected to hold, having assumed she would hold nothing, having assumed a lot of things that week. Ms. Ferreira drove past at six-forty, alone in her car, and slowed, and looked, and did not wave. Autumn raised her sign anyway, a small uncalibrated movement, and Mr. Okonkwo arrived with two carafes and the cups stacked inside each other wrong, so that they came apart all at once and rolled toward the curb like small white wheels, and everyone scrambled after them, laughing, before the store lights came on.

The gym smelled like hot glue and printer toner, and Nolan's poster was curling at the corners because he had printed it at eleven the night before, on the family printer that was older than his sister. His table was third from the doors, between a girl growing mold on purpose and a boy who had built a robot that could not, so far, turn left. In front of Nolan sat three sealed tubes of reddish brown gas in a water bath, and next to the bath, a hot plate that had just decided it was done working for the day.

His project was about equilibrium, which he had typed at the top of the poster in a font he now regretted. The tubes held nitrogen dioxide, the gas his chemistry teacher had waved at from a distance while saying the words "don't drop these." In cold water the gas went pale; in warm water it went dark. The whole point was supposed to be that heat nudged the reaction one way or the other, and Nolan was supposed to explain why, smoothly, to a judge, in under ninety seconds. He had the hot water. He had the ice. He had, at the moment, no hot plate.

"Electricity in the gym is on a timer," the mold girl told him, not unkindly, peeling a banana. "Mr. Prasad says it's so nobody burns the school down. Very torpid of them, if you ask me." She pronounced it like a diagnosis and went back to her fungi.

Nolan carried the cold water bath to the judges' table to ask if there was a kettle anywhere in the building, and while he was gone, the trouble arrived in the form of a kid, maybe ten, with a lanyard that said OBSERVER, who had been circling the tables like a small shark. The kid stopped at the next table over, where a sophomore named Priya had a poster about hydrogen as a fuel. Priya was off arguing with the robot boy about extension cords. The kid picked up her marker and started writing on her tablecloth, which was paper, and which she had not intended as paper for other people.

Nolan came back with a kettle borrowed from the teachers' lounge and found the kid deep in arithmetic. "Two H two," the kid was muttering, "plus O two. That's two of the H-twos, so four hydrogens. And the O two has two oxygens." He counted on the paper. "Then two H two O. Two waters. Two hydrogens each, that's four. One oxygen each, that's two." He looked up at Nolan with the expression of someone who has caught the universe doing something tidy. "It's the same. Both sides."

"That's the idea," Nolan said, setting the kettle down. "Two moles of hydrogen gas, one mole of oxygen gas, two moles of water. Everything you started with shows up at the end."

"Why?"

Nolan opened his mouth and then closed it, because the honest answer was that he was seventeen hours into knowing anything about chemistry at all, and this kid was asking the kind of question that professors wrote whole books avoiding. "Because atoms don't just wander off," he said. "They keep the score even."

Priya returned, saw her tablecloth, and did not scream, which Nolan thought showed real character. "Oh, that's actually useful," she said, crouching to look at the kid's counting. "I've been trying to explain that for two weeks and you did it in marker." She looked up at Nolan. "Is your hot plate dead? I heard about your hot plate. It's the whole gym, apparently. Everyone's talking about your hot plate."

"My hot plate is not interesting enough to be gossip."

"Beguile yourself if you want," Priya said, "but your tubes are the only project in here that changes color, and right now they're all just sitting there being brown."

That was the problem, put plainly. The judges were starting on the far side of the room. He had ice and he had, now, a kettle of lukewarm teachers'-lounge water, and the demonstration needed heat, and his whole understanding of what heat did was one paragraph he had read four times without it ever quite settling into his head. He poured the kettle water into the bath anyway. It was barely warm. The tubes sat there, faintly pink, torpid as Tuesday.

The kid drifted back over, lanyard swinging. "Why do you want them hot?"

"Because I have to explain why they get darker," Nolan said. "And I mostly know that heat pushes it toward the darker stuff, and cold pushes it back, and the system kind of... leans away from whatever you do to it. You add heat, it acts like it's using the heat up. You take heat away, it acts like it's making more." He heard himself say it and stopped. "Wait. Say that again to me."

"Why?"

"No, I mean it. Ask me again why I want them hot."

The kid, game for anything, shrugged. "Why do you want them hot?"

"Because when I push on the equilibrium, it pushes back," Nolan said, and the paragraph he had read four times finally walked into the room and sat down. The system wasn't resisting him out of spite. It was doing exactly what a system with two gases on one side and one on the other could do, shifting its weight the only ways it had available. Heat was a push. Cold was a pull. The color was just the system leaning.

"Mr. Prasad says begging the judges works too," Priya offered. "He said it as a joke but he said it twice, so."

The kettle, plugged into the one live outlet behind the mold empire, began its slow climb toward a boil. Nolan stood over the bath with the kid beside him, both of them watching the pink tubes like they were waiting for something to hatch.

"If it works," the kid said, "do I get credit?"

"You get the marker," Nolan said, and lifted the kettle.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
story:
The quarry had filled with spring rain again, green-black and cold, and Morgan spread the ocean current map across the flat top of a boulder so it wouldn't blow into the water. She weighted the corners with four chunks of limestone, one of them shaped, if you squinted, like a gavel, which she thought was funny because in the fall she was supposed to be deciding between studying oceanography and studying law. Her father had offered to underwrite either degree, which he said in the tone of a man handing over something heavier than money.

The want was simple and specific: in eleven days she had to give a ten-minute presentation at a summer program's intake interview, and the assigned topic was how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. She had a folder of notes, a printed map with arrows curling like spilled hair across the Atlantic, and no speech. What she did have was Dex, who was floating on an inner tube twenty feet out, and her phone, which had one bar of signal at the very edge of the quarry.

"Come be my audience," she called.

"You come be my lifeguard," Dex called back, but he paddled in anyway, dripping, ebullient about having gone in before June, and sat shivering on the boulder while she taped the map to a sunlit slab of rock like a lecturer at the world's least convenient chalkboard.

"Okay," she said. "Warm water leaves the Gulf of Mexico, moves north along the American coast, then swings east across the Atlantic toward Europe." She traced the arrows. "So far so good."

"Very good," said Dex, who was being a generous audience because he wanted her to return the favor at his own interview, which was about a community garden and which he had not started preparing.

"But here's where I keep getting stuck." She unfolded a second printout, a latitude map, and put her finger on London. "London is at about 51.5 degrees north. Farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. More north than the whole US-Canada border line."

Dex leaned in, water running off his elbows onto the paper. "That cannot be right. Winnipeg is cold. London has, like, rain and cafes."

"Look at the line. All of it, every state, sits south of London."

He stared at the map for a long moment, lips moving slightly, and then said, "Okay, that's going in your talk. Start with that. Everyone falls off their chair."

She wrote it in the margin, and then sat down on the limestone because the problem had come into focus. If London sat that far north, its weather should look like a Canadian prairie, and it didn't, and her job was to say why, when the honest answer was that she could trace the arrows but not yet see the whole machine. The current map showed the ocean as if it were a river with a personality, single-minded and helpful, and that felt too easy, like a lawyer who only ever described one side. Her jurisprudence-minded half wanted to cross-examine the map, and her ocean-minded half wanted to trust it, and for eleven days she had let them argue instead of doing the work.

So she did what she could actually do. She spread both maps side by side on the boulder, the currents over the latitudes, and made herself look at them together, not as rivals but as witnesses to the same event. Where the warm arrow crossed toward Europe, the latitude lines ran on indifferent of it. The water went one way, the geometry another, and the talk, she realized, was the space between them: not a claim that the current was kind, only that it carried heat north and east, and that London existed inside that traffic.

She drafted a message to the program director that evening, sitting on the hood of her car above the quarry, and read it aloud to Dex before sending it.

"Dear Dr. Okafor: For my presentation I'd like to begin with the latitude of London, which surprised me, and use it to ask the question honestly rather than answer it completely. I can describe the Gulf Stream's path. What stays uncertain to me is how much of northern Europe's climate it accounts for, and I'd rather say that plainly than pretend certainty I don't have. Is that acceptable for the format? Sincerely, Morgan Reyes."

"Send it," said Dex. "It's the most lawyer thing you've ever written, and the least lawyer thing, at the same time."

She sent it. Then she folded both maps, put the gavel-shaped stone in her pocket for no reason she could defend, and started down the path to the water, where Dex was already shouting that last one in was a rotten egg.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
Thomas had promised his music theory teacher a marked score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, by Monday, and by Saturday afternoon he still could not find the line where the exposition ended and the development began. He sat in the third row of the empty concert hall with the score open on his knees, a pencil behind his ear, and a programme from last night's rehearsal folded into his pocket. The hall smelled of dust and lemon polish, and somewhere above him a workman on a scaffold adjusted a light.

He had a method, or half of one. In theory class they had tried to codify sonata form into three clean boxes: exposition, development, recapitulation. First theme, second theme, closing theme, then the composer took the material apart, then put it back. But the Mozart on the page kept refusing to sit still inside the boxes, and Thomas suspected the problem was his ear rather than the composer's.

"You're the one doing the analysis," said Priya, coming down the aisle with her violin case. She was rehearsing that evening and had let him in on her guest pass. "Any chance you're wrong about where you drew that line?"

"I'm wrong about most of it." He held up the score, its margins already crowded with arrows and crossed-out brackets. "I thought the second theme started at measure twenty-two, but my marks from Thursday say something different, and Thursday me didn't leave a note."

Priya set her case on a seat and leaned over the page. "Sing the beginning," she said. "The very first theme."

He sang it, thin and unsure, and then hummed the passage he had marked as the second theme. Something about the two didn't fit, and he couldn't say why. Priya plucked a string absently, an open A, and the piano in his head rearranged itself around the sound.

"Play it on the guitar," she said. "You brought the guitar, didn't you. You always bring the guitar."

He had, because his guitar teacher had assigned him a melody project and Thomas, whose hands could manage very little, had planned the entire melody around three chords. "The only ones I know," he admitted, taking the case out. "C, F and G. My guitar teacher says the three primary chords of a major key are built on the first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major that's C, F and G. So my melody goes C, F, G, C, F, G, and back." He strummed them, the sound unexpectedly large in the empty hall.

"Play the Mozart first theme over those," Priya said.

He did, slowly, picking out the melody with his right hand while the left dragged from C to F to G. At the second theme he faltered, then stopped. "It doesn't go back to C," he said. "The second theme sits on G. It's the dominant." He looked up. "So in the exposition the second theme is in G, and when it all comes back at the end, it has to come back in C, or it isn't a recapitulation. That's how I find the line. The recapitulation isn't where the tune returns. It's where the tune returns and stays home."

"Mark it," Priya said.

He drew a firm bracket and wrote recap in the margin, and then, following the same logic backwards, found the place where G took over and the material began to scatter. Development, he wrote, and underlined it twice. But at measure fifty-five he stopped again. The first theme reappeared there, whole and familiar, and he almost marked it, except that his left hand was still sitting on F, not C.

"That's a fake," he said quietly. "It comes back in the wrong key. The real one has to be later, in C." He searched forward, bar by bar, humming under his breath, querulous with himself whenever he lost the thread, until at last the theme settled onto the C chord under his fingers and stayed. He drew the final line and sat back, and for a moment neither of them said anything.

"So Monday you hand it in?" Priya asked, closing her case.

"Half of it," Thomas said. "I know where the sections are. I still can't say why Mozart bothers with the fake one, or what the development is doing besides wandering around. My dad thinks I should drop the elective and take immunology instead, something with a clearer syllabus." He laughed a little. "Maybe the wandering is the point. I don't know yet."

He played his three chords once more, C, F and G, then the first theme over them, and the theme sounded different now that he knew where it was going. Priya picked up her case, and as she started up the aisle she called back over her shoulder, "Still here at six. The piano's unlocked."

Thomas folded the score, took out the pencil, and went to find the stage.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
Brody pushed the coffee table against the wall and dragged the armchair to where the imaginary stage lights would be. His mother's living room had become a black box theater, minus the black and minus the box, and by Saturday it had to work as the set for a one-act called "The Long Pause," which Mr. Ferrante's drama class had handed over to him because nobody else wanted the directing credit. He wanted it. He wanted it the way you want something you have never once done.

The trouble announced itself on Tuesday. Dana, who played the older sister, sat on the armchair, and Tomas, who played the brother, stood behind her, and for the entire first scene Brody watched the back of Dana's head while she delivered the best lines in the play. He crouched in the kitchen doorway, which he had decided was row F, seat 11, and squinted.

"Tomas, move," he called.

"Where?"

"I don't know yet."

He tried Tomas on the left, then on the right, then kneeling like a man proposing, which made Dana laugh so hard she dropped a page of script. Nothing solved it. Her face stayed aimed at the couch, at the window, at the fake fourth wall, anywhere but at the seats where an audience would sit.

That night he texted his cousin Priya, who had done a summer intensive at a theater in the city. She answered at eleven with a voice memo, and he played it twice while lying on the floor of his room. "You want them to cheat out," she said, sounding half asleep. "Cheating out means the actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while they're talking to the other character, so their face and voice carry." He lay there wondering why nobody had ever told him that bodies could lie, could point one direction and intend another, and whether that was a skill or a kind of honesty he hadn't learned yet.

Wednesday he made Dana and Tomas run the scene again. "Cheat out," he said, tapping his own collarbone to show the angle. Dana swiveled maybe ten degrees toward the doorway. Tomas, who was garrulous by nature and panicked in silence, filled the pause with a speech about how weird it felt.

"It's supposed to feel weird," Brody said. "It's not natural. Real people face each other."

"Then why?"

Because the room isn't real either, Brody thought, and the lights aren't real, and the sister isn't her sister. He didn't say any of that. He said, "Just try it twice and then argue with me."

They ran it. From the kitchen doorway, Dana's face opened up like a door she'd been keeping her shoulder against. Her voice reached him without strain, and the line about the empty bedroom at the end of the hall landed for the first time in a way that made his stomach drop. Tomas cheated out too far, nearly facing the seats, and Brody spent ten minutes adjusting him in small increments, hand hovering near his elbow, like tuning something he couldn't see.

Thursday, a new problem. Cheated out, the two of them looked composed, deliberate, almost formal, and the scene was supposed to be a fight between siblings who knew each other's worst memories. The geometry that made them visible made them careful. Brody sat on the floor with the script and thought about his math homework, about how a lemma was a small thing you proved first so that a bigger proof could stand on it. The angle was like that. It was true, it worked, it carried the voice, but it couldn't be the whole argument. He needed it to hold without anyone noticing it holding.

So he let the fight break the rule on purpose. When Dana stood up and turned her full back to the seats, shouting at Tomas face to face, the sudden wrongness of it did something the angle never could. Then she cheated back out for the quiet last line, and the turn itself became part of the scene, a pivot from fury to something smaller and more exposed.

"Did you plan that?" Tomas asked.

"No," Brody said, and then, honestly, "Sort of. I planned that something like it might happen."

Friday night his mother watched from the stairs with a mug of tea, and Priya, home for the weekend, took the kitchen doorway seat without being told it was his. The run enraptured him so completely that he forgot to take notes, forgot he was supposed to be the one with the pencil, forgot everything except Dana turning ten degrees toward the dark where an audience would breathe.

Afterward Priya said, "The turn at the end. You mean that?"

"I don't know yet," Brody said. "Ask me after Saturday."

He gathered the scattered pages of script off the carpet, squared them against his knee, and set them face down on the armchair where Dana would sit.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
story:
The morning her mother sent her to the market, Maika still smelled of the airplane she'd taken three days earlier, after the call came, after the funeral that had blurred past her like scenery from a train window. Her mother pressed folded bills into her hand and said, "Marigolds. The big orange ones, as many as you can carry. Your grandmother would want the altar right." Then her aunt Rosa had come along, and now the two of them stood in the flower section of the Mercado de Jamaica, where the aisles had been drowned in color overnight, buckets of gladiolas and chrysanthemums and velvet-red roses jammed shoulder to shoulder.

Every stall had flowers; not every stall had the right ones. The first vendor shook his head. The second had a crate of marigolds so pale they looked jaundiced, more yellow than orange, their scent thin and greenish. Maika set her jaw and kept walking. Her mother's instructions had been specific, and specificity was the only thing Maika could offer now, since she could not offer grief of the correct size or tears at the correct hour. She had cried on the plane, sideways against the window, and then stopped, and felt ever since that she was doing this wrong.

"Why does it have to be those?" she asked her aunt, when the third stall also failed them. "They're just flowers. She liked lilies too, she had that painting of lilies in the hallway."

"They're called cempasúchil," her aunt said, lifting a stray stem off the wet floor and handing it back to a vendor. "For the Day of the Dead. The bright color and the strong scent, they say the souls follow them home." She said it lightly, the way she said most things, and then moved on to argue with a man about the price of pan de muerto, leaving Maika standing there with the sentence still settling on her.

Souls follow them home. Maika turned the idea over as they walked, aisle after aisle, her arms beginning to ache from the candles and the sugar skulls and the rolls of papel picado her aunt kept acquiring. At home in California, her grandmother had been a person reduced to phone calls and a genealogy of habits: always asking about grades, always sending sweaters two sizes too large. Here she was a house, a street, a language Maika spoke with an accent she could hear herself. Her mother believed the altar mattered in one way, as obligation and inheritance; her aunt seemed to believe it mattered in another, as a practical arrangement, scent and color, a path laid down for a traveler. Maika did not know which version she held, or whether holding both at once was dishonest. She only knew she was not going back without real marigolds, the deep orange ones that stained your fingers when you pulled them apart.

They found the last good bunch at a stall near the loading dock, an old woman selling out of a bucket she was about to carry back to her truck. Maika paid too much for them and did not care. On the bus she held the flowers in her lap, and the smell rose off them, bitter and sweet at once, nothing like lilies, and she caught herself breathing carefully, as though inhaling them was a task with a technique. Outside the window the city went by, and she thought about a soul finding its way, about whether her grandmother, who had gotten lost driving to Maika's school once in a rental car, could navigate by smell across whatever distance this was.

At the house, the altar was half built on the dining table that nobody had eaten at in years. Her mother had set out the photograph, the one from before, and a cup of the coffee her grandmother drank all day, and the small clay dog Maika had made in second grade that had somehow survived a decade in this house. Maika went to the kitchen to cut the marigold stems, and while she worked, her cousin Timo motioned to her from the back door.

"Come see," he said.

The backyard was small and wild, the pots her grandmother had tended gone leafy and loose since the hospital, since everything. Along the back wall, in a cracked cement planter Maika had never once looked at, a whole row of marigolds had gone over, unwatered for weeks, and beyond them, self-seeded into the dirt path, dozens more, the deepest orange she had seen all day, glowing in the late light. Her grandmother had planted them herself, sometime in the summer, before anyone knew. Timo crouched and snapped one off at the stem and held it up.

"She didn't need us to buy her anything," he said. "She already knew the way."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
story:
Raphael had never been the kind of person to make a fuss about money, which is why he was standing at the bank at nine in the morning making a fuss about money. The branch on Marsh Street smelled like carpet cleaner and cold coffee, and the woman behind the counter, whose name tag said DOREEN, looked at him the way people look at weather they can't do anything about. He slid his statement across the marble. "This says my savings earned eleven dollars," he said. "That can't be right. There's barely anything in there."

Doreen turned the paper toward herself. "Four hundred and twenty dollars at, let's see, the rate they give students. Interest gets added, and then the interest earns its own interest. That's why it goes faster than you'd think." She said it the way a person says the bus comes at seven, a fact of the world, not a philosophy. Raphael, who had opened the account three years ago with birthday money and then mostly forgotten it, felt something shift in him, small and turbid, like sediment stirred up from the bottom of a clear glass. He had always believed he was attentive. He had, in fact, once told his cousin that he "tracked every dollar," a claim he now reviewed with some discomfort, since four hundred and twenty of those dollars had been sitting in the dark earning wages without his knowledge.

The real problem was the deposit for his off-campus room, eight hundred dollars, due in two weeks, and the fact that his checking account held sixty-one dollars and a memory of a night in June when he and Felix had driven to the coast on a whim he still declined to call an impulse. It had been a plan, he would have said. Plans could be last-minute. His uncle Marcus had offered the money over the phone in April, in that voice he used that made generosity sound like a contract. "Six hundred, five percent, two years, simple," Marcus had said. "You pay back the principal and the interest, that's it. Family rate."

Raphael had said yes immediately, because he was decisive, and also because he had no idea what any of it meant. He'd been meaning to work it out ever since. Now, in the vinyl chair by the brochures, he borrowed a pen from Doreen's cup and did the arithmetic on the back of his statement. Principal times rate times time. Six hundred, times five percent, times two years. Thirty dollars a year, sixty dollars total. He wrote it twice to be sure. Six hundred sixty, and he was done. It was, he had to admit, less terrifying than the word "loan" had sounded in April, sitting in Marcus's kitchen while his uncle cut an apple into slices with unnecessary precision.

The trouble was that Marcus wasn't the only option. Doreen, when he wandered back to her window to return the pen, mentioned that the bank did small personal loans, and that the rates were "not what I'd call friendly for someone with your file." Raphael asked what his file said. "Sixty-one dollars," she said, not unkindly, and a man in line behind him laughed, and Raphael laughed too, because it was funny, objectively, that a person could be eighteen and have a file. He was not, he told himself, embarrassed. He was a person who could laugh at himself. This was a quality he valued, along with decisiveness, and with never making a fuss, both of which he was demonstrating beautifully this morning.

He sat down again among the brochures and tried to hold both offers in his head at once, which was like holding two fish. Marcus's money was cheap, sixty dollars over two years, math he could do on a bank statement with a borrowed pen. But the bank's savings interest, that quiet compounding, had turned his forgotten four hundred and twenty into four hundred thirty-one without him lifting a finger, and he suspected, though he couldn't prove it, that a bank loan would compound too, each month's interest birthing the next month's, a mechanism both marvelous and faintly predatory. He refused to predicate his choice on which lender liked him more. Marcus's affection was an artifice he'd learned to see through years ago, the loans to cousins at Thanksgiving, the ledger he kept in his head and consulted at funerals. The bank, at least, put its appetite in writing.

On the other hand, family debt had a shape bank debt didn't. Six hundred sixty to Marcus meant dinners where his uncle would mention, gently, that Raphael was good for it, and Raphael's mother pressing her napkin flat. Sixty dollars was the price of the money, but the price of the owing was something the formula didn't cover. He could feel both truths and he could not make them add up. Perhaps the honest position was that he didn't know yet what kind of borrower he was, or whether the version of himself who drove to the coast in June was the exception or the rule. He wrote SIX-SIXTY on the statement and underlined it, then, feeling that underlining was itself a small performance of decisiveness, crossed it out.

He texted Marcus from the sidewalk outside: I'll take it, and I already know it's six sixty total, so don't round up at Thanksgiving. Marcus replied with a single thumbs-up, which Raphael chose to read as respect.

He was unlocking his bike when Felix came around the corner, backpack sagging, face arranged into its asking configuration. "Buddy. Small thing. Two hundred for books, I'll pay you back by December, promise." Raphael felt the words assemble themselves before he could stop them, the formula already running, two hundred, times some rate he'd invent, times a term. "Four percent," he heard himself say. "Simple. Nothing fancy." Felix stared at him. "Since when do you charge interest?" Raphael clipped his helmet strap and swung a leg over the frame. "Since I got a file at the bank," he said, and rode off down Marsh Street with the pen still in his jacket pocket.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
story:
The skate park at six was all long shadows and grinding wheels, and James sat on the flat bottom of the bowl with a physics worksheet folded in his back pocket, half of it already soft with sweat. He had come to watch Rio launch off the coping, but he kept taking the paper out, because the problem refused to behave: a ball leaves the ground at fourteen meters per second at some angle, level ground, no air resistance, and he was supposed to find how long it stays in the air. He had found the vertical part, ten meters per second up, and he had divided by g, which was 9.8, and gotten about one second. Then he had written it in the answer blank. Something about it felt thin.

Rio dropped in, pumped twice, and rose off the lip into the air, board spinning under him. James watched the height of it, the pause at the top where the board seemed to consider its options, and then the fall. He looked back at his number. One second to get up there. But Rio came down after that. The flight wasn't just the rising. It was rising and falling, and if you only counted the climb you were describing half a jump.

"You're doing homework at a skate park," Rio said, rolling over and flipping his board up into his hand.

"Projectile motion," James said. "Supposed to be like this." He nodded at the bowl. "You're the projectile."

"Flattering." Rio squinted at the worksheet. "So what's wrong?"

"Everything's on level ground, no air resistance, which is nothing like you. But I got one second for the whole flight and it feels short." He traced the arc Rio had just made in the air with his finger, up and over. "It took you about that long just going up."

Rio stood with the board under his arm and watched a younger kid push tentatively along the top of the quarter pipe, as if the drop-in might portend something irreversible, which, on a board, it often did. "So count the way down too."

"It's not just counting it. The way down takes the same time as the way up. Exactly the same." James said it and then tested it in his mouth, unsure. Was that true, or was it only true without air, without the friction of the world? He turned the pen over. In the clean world of the problem, rising and falling were mirror images, so the time to the top was half the flight. He wrote two seconds, then crossed it out and wrote the division again, ten divided by 9.8, times two, and got a little over two seconds for the whole jump. From where Dara was sitting, up on the platform with her helmet still on, it looked like the answer had startled him.

She had been half listening while re-lacing her shoes, the way she half listened to most things, filing them for later. But she noticed him sit up straighter, noticed the pen stop moving, and she was curious in the specific way she got curious, which was sideways. She skated over and set her board down.

"What did you find?"

"That I was answering the wrong question," James said. "I found the time to the top of the arc and forgot the fall."

"Is that cheating?"

"It's physics. On level ground with no air, the time of flight is twice the initial vertical velocity divided by g. Rising and falling take equal times." He said it plainly, like reading a street sign, and shrugged. "That's all it is."

Dara tilted her head. She had a whole lineage of skaters behind her, an older cousin who had taught her that tricks were passed down person to person like stories, and she thought physics might work the same way, except the stories were about numbers. "So the whole flight is just the up part doubled."

"Twice the vertical part. The sideways part doesn't even matter for time." He looked at Rio. "When you clear that gap by the fence, how fast you're moving forward changes how far you go. It doesn't change how long you're in the air."

Rio rolled the board under his foot, considering. He dropped in without answering, pumped the transition, and shot off the lip into the still evening air. James watched the whole arc this time, up, the pause, down, and tried to see the two halves of it laid over each other, equal and silent. Dara counted under her breath, "one one-thousand, two one-thousand," and got to a little past two when the wheels touched concrete.

"Close enough," she said, and pushed off toward the bowl.
